3.18.20 The Department, in its submission on legislative reforms, provided that i t is 
proposed to bring following amendments in the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 for Ease 
of Doing Business: - 
 
a. Modify definition of unsafe food to avoid contradictory implementation of provisions 
of the Act: The term Mis -Branded and Sub-standard as defined in FSS Act, 2006 says 
that it does not render the article of food unsafe. Selling of Sub- standard/ Mis- branded 
food may lead to adjudication (civil court) while selling unsafe food may lead to 
prosecution. Such contradictory/ambiguous definition of unsafe food leads to 
individual discretion an d regulatory unpredictability for FBOs in case of non -
compliance.   
 

113 
 
b. Exemption to retailers/ distributors from penalty for non -compliances beyond their 
control: As per the Section 49 of FSS Act, 2006 on General Provisions relating to 
penalty, in case of no n-compliance, penalty is applicable to all FBOs such as seller, 
distributor, manufacturer etc.  But, the retailers/ aggregators/ distributors of pre -
packaged food products have limited role in ensuring the kind of additives/ ingredients 
used and the level at which they are used.  
 
c. Provision for compounding of offences: As per Section 69 of FSS Act, 2006, power to 
compound offences is presently applicable only to registered Food Business Operators 
(FBOs). However, licensed FBOs committing minor offences are s till required to 
undergo adjudication proceedings, as no provision for compounding is currently 
available to them.  
 
d. Enabling use of all food grade solvents for plants and botanical extract: As per Section 
22 of FSS Act, 2006, plants or botanicals extracts are allowed in only 3 solvents (water, 
ethyl alcohol or hydro alcoholic extract)  and/or its combination. The Act was passed in 
2006. Since then, significant technological advancement has taken place necessitating 
use of wide range of solvents. This provis ion is now restricting the scope of innovation 
by the industry.  
 
3.18.21 The Committee notes with serious concern the stark regional disparity in 
the availability of FSSAI -notified testing infrastructure. While states like Maharashtra, 
Tamil Nadu, and Gujarat have a high concentration of facilities, some States and Union 
Territories, namely, Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram, Sikkim, Andaman & Nicobar 
Islands, Chandigarh, Ladakh, Puducherry and Lakshadweep lack even a single notified 
laboratory. Furthermore, Refe rral Food Laboratories are restricted to just 11 states 
namely, Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Haryana, Karnataka, Kerala, Maharashtra, Punjab, 
Tamil Nadu, Telangana, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal. The Committee believes that 
such skewed distribution severely un dermines the equitable enforcement of food safety 
standards nationwide. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department 
immediately prioritize the unrepresented States and UTs for the deployment of the 
pending 236 "next -generation" Mobile Food Tes ting Labs (MFTLs) once their 
specifications are finalized by May 2026. Concurrently, the Department must allocate 
targeted financial assistance to establish permanent, state -owned primary and referral 
laboratories in the North -Eastern states and UTs to eli minate their dependency on 
distant facilities. 
 
3.18.22 The Committee is of the view that robust regulatory frameworks are 
rendered ineffective without adequate manpower and institutional grievance 
mechanisms. The Committee observes that out of FSSAI's 822  sanctioned posts, 279 
(nearly 34%) remain vacant, perpetuating an undesirable reliance on contractual staff. 
Additionally, the complete absence of Food Safety Appellate Tribunals in Andhra 
Pradesh and Dadra and Nagar Haveli & Daman & Diu, along with the d elayed 
constitution in Bihar, Karnataka, and Mizoram, deprives citizens and Food Business 
Operators (FBOs) of essential, timely legal recourse. The Committee, therefore, 

114 
 
recommends that the Department initiate a fast -track, time-bound recruitment drive in 
coordination with the relevant recruiting agencies to fill the 279 vacancies at FSSAI. 
Furthermore, the Department must proactively engage with the defaulting State/UT 
governments to ensure the immediate constitution and operationalization of their 
respective Food Safety Appellate Tribunals. 
 
3.18.23 The Committee believes that the proposed legislative amendments to the 
Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, are critical for modernizing the regulatory 
landscape. The current statutory ambiguities, such as pena lizing retailers for 
manufacturing-level non-compliances beyond their control, restricting the compounding 
of minor offences only to registered (and not licensed) FBOs, and limiting botanical 
extractions to outdated solvent technologies, create unnecessary  compliance burdens 
and stifle industry innovation. The Committee is of the view that redefining "unsafe 
food" to remove contradictory interpretations and expanding permissible food -grade 
solvents will significantly enhance operational predictability. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Department expedite the drafting and parliamentary introduction 
of these legislative amendments to ensure that the statutory framework aligns with 
contemporary technological realities and fair regulatory practices. 
 
National Medical commission 
 
3.18.24 National Medical Commission (NMC) was established under the provisions of 
the National Medical Commission Act, 2019, superseding the erstwhile Medical Council of 
India (MCI). The Commission is entrusted with prescribi ng policies and standards for 
undergraduate and postgraduate medical education, regulating medical institutions, 
maintaining the national medical register, and ensuring ethical conduct among registered 
practitioners. Its functioning is carried out through autonomous boards namely: (a) 
Undergraduate Medical Education Board (UGMEB); (b) Postgraduate Medical Education 
Board (PGMEB); (c) Medical Assessment and Rating Board (MARB); and (d) Ethics and 
Medical Registration Board (EMRB). 
3.18.25 On being asked abou t achievements, the Department submitted that during the 
financial year 2025 -26, National Medical Commission (NMC), recorded substantial physical

the view that such restrictive practices act as a significant barrier to the mobility of

burden on candidates. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department, in 
coordination with the upcoming National Dental Commission (NDC), issue a mandatory 
directive to all State Health Secretaries and Directorates of Medical Education ensuring 
that inter-state registration is recognized during the application and examination stages, 
with the provision that successful candidates may transfer their registration  under

3.18.35 The Committee observes a critical depletion in the human resource 
capacity of the Dental Council of India, with 47 out of 95 sanctioned posts currently 
vacant, representing a nearly 50% vacancy rate. The Co mmittee believes that the 
instruction in the year 2023 to halt fresh regular recruitment, while intended to facilitate 
the transition to the National Dental Commission (NDC), has resulted in an 
administrative vacuum that threatens the quality of regulatory  oversight and the 
processing of Letters of Permission (LOPs) for BDS and MDS courses. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Department prioritize the early constitution and 
operationalization of the National Dental Commission (NDC) as mandated by the NDC 
Act, 2023. The Committee is of the view that the swift establishment of the 
Commission‘s permanent organisation al and administrative structure is the only 
sustainable way to fill this regulatory void and resolve the current staffing crisis, 
ensuring that the quality and affordability of dental education are not compromised 
during this prolonged transitional phase. Till the constitution of NDC, the Department 
may consider a special "Transition Recruitment Plan" or the deputation of personnel 
from other health departments.

3.19.5 The Committee notes with appreciation the satisfactory utilization of  budgetary 
funds by AIIMS, New Delhi, and acknowledges the gradual increase in the Budget 
Estimate (BE) to ₹5500.92 crore for FY 2026 -27. However, the Committee observes that 
this allocation falls short of the Institute's projected requirement of ₹5758 cro re. The 
Committee believes that fully funding the Institute is non -negotiable, especially as 
AIIMS is executing a complex, 190 -acre integrated Master Plan while simultaneously 
maintaining unhindered patient care services. The Committee, therefore, recommen ds 
that the Department proactively review and enhance the allocation at the Revised 
Estimate (RE) stage to bridge this ₹257 crore deficit. Ensuring adequate liquidity is 
critical to support not only the ongoing phased redevelopment but also the smooth 
initiation of upcoming mega -projects, such as establishment of a CBRNE facility and 
expansion of JPNATC and Centre of Excellence in Child Health at Jhajjar. 
 
3.19.6 The Committee views with serious concern the severe procedural bottlenecks 
stalling vital patie nt-care infrastructure. Specifically, the Committee notes that the 
Super Specialty OPD Block at Masjid Moth is caught in a prolonged DoE reappraisal 
loop due to tender costs exceeding the ₹500 crore threshold, while the 150 -bedded 
Critical Care Block is se verely delayed by pending tree transplantation approvals and 
shifting Environmental Clearance (EC) goalposts by the MoEF&CC. The Committee is 
of the view that such bureaucratic delays defeats the urgent mandate of these projects. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department immediately constitute an 
empowered Inter-Ministerial Steering Group to aggressively liaise with the Department 
of Expenditure (DoE), MoEF&CC, and the Delhi Government. This group must secure 
a specialized, fast -track clearan ce pathway for all AIIMS infrastructural projects to 
prevent further cost escalations and time overruns. 
 
3.19.7 The Committee observes a significant failure in the initial planning and inter -
agency coordination regarding the ₹4441 crore Redevelopment of Residential Colonies 
project. The Committee believes that the Delhi Development Authority's (DDA) 
rejection of the commercial monetization of the West Ansari Nagar (WAN) campus, 
which formed the very basis of the project's self -financing model, has severely derailed 
the initiative. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department urgently 
finalize and submit the revised Cabinet Note with a realistic, updated financial structure 
that does not rely on contested land -use conversions. Furthermore, the Committee is of 
the view that while the revised financial model is being approved, the Department must 
ensure uninterrupted funding so that the ongoing construction of the Type IV and Type 
V quarters (costing ₹118.92 crore and ₹143.94 crore, respectively) meets their stipulated 
completion deadlines of 2026 and 2027. 
 
3.19.8 The Committee notes with concern the p rofound lack of progress in critical 
projects, specifically the Expansion of the National Drug Dependence Treatment Centre 
(NDDTC) and the establishment of the ₹358.19 crore IT and Network Security 
Infrastructure. Despite the project‘s official commencemen t dated of 18 th March 2024 
with 18 -month completion timeline and an advance payment of ₹8.60 crore to the 
CPWD for the NDDTC, physical progress remains at 'Nil', while the ambitious IT 

122 
 
modernization project faces an exceptionally tight completion deadline of September 
2026, given the complexity of digitizing a massive healthcare ecosystem. The Committee 
believes that such delays in both civil works for vulnerable populations and the digital 
resilience of the Institute‘s data systems are unacceptable in a pr emier national 
institution. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department institute a 
unified "High-Level Project Monitoring Cell" to hold both civil executing agencies (like 
CPWD) and technical consultants (like BEL) strictly accountable throug h monthly 
milestone tracking. The Committee is of the view that the Department must formulate 
and enforce penalty clauses in MoUs to held executing agencies financially accountable 
for construction inertia. The Committee further urges the Department to est ablish a 
dedicated Cyber -Security Cell within AIIMS to manage and protect the new digital 
infrastructure from the increasing global threats to healthcare data. 
 
3.19.9 The Committee observes that while AIIMS, New Delhi is undergoing a massive 
internal redevelopment, its role in decompressing tertiary care through satellite facilities 
remains behind schedule. Specifically, the construction of the 30 -bedded Community 
Health Centre at Fatehpur Billoch and the New Ward Block at CRHSP Ballabhgarh are 
both trailing their original stipulated completion dates, with the latter showing a dismal 
physical progress of only 15% nearly a year after its start. The Committee believes that 
the chronic overcrowding at the main Ansari Nagar campus can only be permanently 
mitigated if these peripheral and community -based facilities are operationalized to 
handle primary and secondary workloads. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the Department institute a "Satellite Project Acceleration Taskforce" to oversee these 
specific expansions and ensure their timely completion, thereby guaranteeing that rural 
and semi-urban populations gain access to AIIMS -standard care without necessitating 
travel to the high-burden New Delhi facility.

3.19.15 The Committee observes with concern a staggering 35% vacancy rate (452

members joined the institute during this period. The Committee believes that this 
recruitment paralysis severely jeopardizes the academic and clinical standards of India's 
premier medical institution. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
Department launch a focused, time -bound recruitment drive with clear milestones, for 
example, target filling (at least 85%) of sanctioned posts by fast -tracking advertised 
vacancies, conducting rolling interview panels, and decentralising selection timelines to 
avoid protracted offer -to-joining delays. T he 328 currently advertised faculty positions 
may be finalised within the first two quarters of FY 2026 -27. Furthermore, the 
Committee is of the view that the persistent reliance on contractual faculty (currently 73 
Assistant Professors) must be phased out in favor of permanent appointments to ensure 
institutional belongingness and long -term accountability, as contractual arrangements 
should serve only as temporary stop -gap measures. L ong-standing contractual 
incumbents meeting eligibility criteria should be offered a regularisation/absorption 
pathway. The Department should introduce retention incentives tied to hard -to-fill 
specialties and underserved postings to improve the offer-to-joining ratio. 
3.19.16 The Committee is concerned about excessive continuous duty hours for 
Junior and Senior Residents and the risk of clinical errors and burnout, thereby 
compromising patient safety . The Comm ittee, therefore, recommends that the 
Department formulate and strictly enforce a "Clinical Duty Hours Regulation" policy 
with mandatory rest periods, and monitored rosters , drawing a direct analogy from 
other safety-critical professions  like civil aviatio n to prevent fatigue -induced accidents.

The presence of senior faculty should be ensured in wards and in operating theatres 
during peak hours by aligning faculty schedules with clinical demand and by appointing 
designated supervisory rosters. Structured m entorship and protected teaching time 
should be introduced so that trainees gain supervised clinical experience rather than 
learning by trial. Additionally, to ensure the retention of high -quality talent, the 
Committee recommends that medical professionals  be provided with improved working 
conditions, including accommodation, transportation, and administrative support, on 
par with the facilities afforded to senior civil servants, and transparent career 
progression with time -bound promotions. The Committee a lso suggests the integration 
of Yoga and the Indian Knowledge System (IKS) within the workforce to address the 
rising incidence of depression and psychiatric issues among the medical community. 
3.19.17 The Committee notes that AIIMS, New Delhi, continues t o struggle with 
high patient loads in OPD and Emergency services, leading to long waiting times (may 
extended to several months) for investigations and surgeries; and optimum and 
uninterrupted supply of drugs and consumables. The Committee believes that ph ysical 
infrastructure alone cannot solve the congestion at a tertiary care center of this scale. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends the immediate implementation of the proposed 
"Digital Command and Control System" and ―Performance -Based Accountability‖, 
utilizing AI -driven analytics to forecast patient demand and optimize surgical 
scheduling, and identifying bottlenecks so that human resources match infrastructure 
growth. Furthermore, the Committee is of the view that a robust digital triage tool must 
be deployed to strengthen the referral system, effectively redirecting non -tertiary cases 
to appropriate secondary centers. This will ensure that the specialized resources of 
AIIMS are reserved for the most complex clinical cases, thereby improving overall 
operational efficiency and patient satisfaction. 
3.19.18 The Committee believes that while AIIMS, New Delhi, currently captures 
extensive hospital utilization and service -delivery statistics, the existing internal 
monitoring mechanism lacks the necessary ext ernal validation to drive systemic 
improvements. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department facilitate 
an independent audit to evaluate hospital -level allocations, utilisation and service 
delivery, and key performance indicators like bed occu pancy rates, bed turnover rates, 
and average length of stay, ICU admissions, surgical volumes, laboratory and 
radiological investigations, hospital infection rate including healthcare associated 
infections, on quarterly basis. The Committee is of the view that the outcomes of these 
audits must be subjected to public scrutiny to ensure absolute institutional transparency 
with audit results directly informing the strategic allocation of resources and the 
planning. 
3.19.19 The Committee believes that the gover nance of a massive, multi -specialty 
ecosystem like AIIMS requires a blend of clinical expertise and formal administrative 
training. The Committee, therefore, recommends that doctors with specialized 
managerial qualifications be prioritized for top -tier pol icy-making and administrative 
positions within the Institute. Additionally, the Committee is of the view that the medical

and nursing curriculum must be reformed to include an introductory syllabus on Ayush

complement allopathic treatments through palliative and preventive care but will also

concludes that this multidisciplinary approach is essent ial for producing a more holistic 
and resilient healthcare workforce.

recommends that the Department consider developing a structured database to assess 
the extent to  which trained specialists contribute to the domestic healthcare system, 
identify gaps in specialist availability across regions, and inform future policy decisions 
relating to medical education, workforce planning and retention of highly skilled 
professionals within the country. 
3.19.30 The Committee notes that the Institute incurred substantial expenditure 
on electricity (₹108.86 crore) and water (₹3.97 crore) during FY 2024 –25, reflecting the

the Institute to enhance solar power generation capacity from 703 KWp to 1108 KWp, 
along with ongoing rooftop solar projects across various blocks and centres, as well as 
measures such as rainwater harvesting and reuse of treated water through sewage 
treatment plants (STPs) for horticulture purposes. While these initiatives are 
encouraging, the Committee is of the view that there remains considerable scope to 
further strengthen sustainable energy and water management practices within the 
Institute. The Co mmittee, therefore, recommends that the Department encourage 
expansion of renewable energy capacity, adoption of energy -efficient technologies, and 
systematic water conservation measures, with clearly defined targets for reducing 
dependence on conventional  electricity and fresh water consumption. Such measures 
would not only reduce operational expenditure in the long term but also promote 
environmentally sustainable practices in large public healthcare institutions.

3.20.5 On a query related to key concern areas of the Institute, the Department submitted that 
the key concern areas of PGIMER, Chandigarh for optimum functioning are Patient load, 
Computerization/digitization, and Manpower. Strategic  measures for efficient functioning of 
the hospital are as follows: 
a) Patient load – PGIMER is in the process of commissioning two new centres namely 
Neurosciences Centre and Mother & Child Health Care Centre alongwith three Satellite 
Centres at Sangrur, Ferozepur and UNA to de-congest the current infrastructure. 
b) The peripheral health care facilities need to be upgraded and a scientific referral system 
be put into place so as to ensure that only genuine patients are referred to PGIMER.   
This will help in de-congesting PGIMER and also hugely benefit the patients.   
c) The current Hospital Information System (HIS) needs to be upgraded. This will help in 
digitizing several manual processes and also the record keeping. 
d) Manpower recruitment to be done to successfully commission the new Centres and fill 
gaps in the current status. 
Several steps are taken to evaluate the service delivery like Mortality meetings, Hospital 
Infection Control Committee meetings, Antibiotic Stewardship Programme, and Patient 
feedback. 24x7 Control Room by Department of Hospital Administration to monitor services. 
 
3.20.6 The Committee notes with concern the protracted delays in operationalizing 
critical facilities, specifically the 300 -bedded Advanced Neurosciences Centre and the 
Advanced Mother & Child Centre, which have been under construction since 2019 and 
2021 respectively, yet remain stalled at 99% and 97% completion. The Committee 
believes that the cited administrative bottlenecks, such as delayed statutory clearances, 
late site handovers, and utility shifting disputes, must be aggressively resolved through a 
dedicated inter -agency task force to prevent further cost escalations. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Department immediately facilitate the final 
commissioning of thes e near -complete projects to directly benefit patient care. 
Furthermore, the Committee is of the view that the budgetary allocation of ₹2504.65 
crore for FY 2026 -27, which falls significantly short of the Institute's projected demand 
of ₹2865.00 crore, must be augmented at the Revised Estimate (RE) stage. This financial 
reinforcement is vital to ensure the smooth initiation of the proposed ₹472.00 crore 
Sarangpur campus (Phase-I) without financially starving the ongoing satellite projects. 
 
3.20.7 The Commit tee observes that the main campus of PGIMER is severely 
overburdened, compromising the quality of specialized tertiary care. The Committee is 
of the view that merely constructing physical satellite centres at Una, Ferozepur, and 

132 
 
Sangrur is insufficient unl ess coupled with a formalized, policy -driven network linking 
these facilities. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department mandate 
the immediate development and implementation of a digitized "scientific referral 
system" across the neighboring states. This system must actively upgrade peripheral 
health facilities to act as primary gatekeepers, utilizing strict digital triage protocols to 
filter and redirect non -tertiary cases. By doing so, the highly specialized resources and 
personnel of PGIMER  will be exclusively reserved for genuine, complex clinical 
interventions, thereby effectively decongesting the institute. 
 
3.20.8 The Committee believes that the successful integration of the five new major 
clinical and satellite centres relies entirely o n concurrent advancements in digital 
infrastructure and human resources. The current reliance on manual processes and an 
outdated Hospital Information System (HIS) hampers both clinical efficiency and data -
driven decision-making. The Committee, therefore, recommends the immediate funding 
and expedited rollout of a modernized, comprehensive HIS to fully digitize record -
keeping, streamline patient flow, and enhance real -time monitoring through existing 
mechanisms like the 24x7 Control Room. The Committee is f urther of the view that the 
Department must authorize a dedicated, time -bound recruitment drive to be executed 
prior to the final handover of the new Neurosciences and Mother & Child centres. It is 
imperative that no newly constructed, state -of-the-art fac ility remains non -operational 
or underutilized due to a preventable shortage of specialized medical and paramedical 
staff.

Department mandate the expedited, institute -wide rollout of the token and Scan -and-

Furthermore, the Committee recommends the establishment of a un ified 'Patient 
Experience Cell' to consolidate data from all feedback streams into a single monthly 
analytical report for the Director, which may be available for public view also, ensuring 
that patient grievances systematically drive operational improvements.

3.21.7 The Committee notes that the Budget Estimate (BE) for 2024 –25 was ₹1440.00 
crore, which was reduced to ₹1370.00 crore at the RE stage, with an a ctual expenditure 
of ₹1351.96 crore, while for 2025 –26 the BE of ₹1450.00 crore was revised to ₹1460.79 
crore, against which the expenditure as on 31.01.2026 stands at ₹1087.52 crore, 
indicating comparatively lower utilisation during the year. Although the  BE for 2026–27 
has been increased to ₹1496.46 crore, against projected requirement of ₹1546.46 crore, 
reflecting growing operational and infrastructure demands. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Department ensure timely release and optimal uti lisation of funds, 
while also strengthening internal monitoring mechanisms for infrastructure projects and 
institutional expenditure so that sanctioned allocations translate into timely completion 
of projects and improved healthcare delivery capacity. 
 
3.21.8 The Committee notes the progress of several infrastructure projects at 
Jawaharlal Institute of Postgraduate Medical Education and Research, Puducherry, 
including the Regional Cancer Centre annexe building, critical care hospital block, 
residential quar ters and the proposed 476 -bedded teaching hospital at the Karaikal 
campus. While some projects are nearing completion, others are still at relatively early 
stages of physical progress. Given the rising burden of non -communicable diseases 
(NCDs), particular ly cancer and cardiovascular diseases, and the existing shortage of 
inpatient beds, operation theatre capacity and cardiac intervention facilities, the 
Committee stresses the need for expedited completion of ongoing infrastructure projects 
and timely approval of new residential and clinical facilities. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Department prioritize the immediate operationalization of the 
Regional Cancer Centre Annexe, which currently stands at 99% physical progress. 
Furthermore, the Com mittee believes that the Institute must aggressively fast -track the 
development of the Sedrapet Campus. Shifting trauma and transplant cases to that 
dedicated 50 -acre satellite facility is paramount to effectively decongesting the main 
campus and freeing u p critical operating theatre (OT) space for elective and specialized 
NCD surgeries. 
 
3.21.9 The Committee notes that while JIPMER has outlined comprehensive structural 
expansions to manage its disproportionate NCD burden and trauma influx, the mere 
addition of physical infrastructure at the main and Sedrapet campuses will not 
autonomously resolve the systemic waitlists and bed deficits. The Committee believes 
that these expansions must be inextricably linked to rigorous, real -time performance 
auditing to pr event the new specialized centres from succumbing to the same 
operational bottlenecks currently congesting the existing facilities. 
 
3.21.10 The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department mandate the 
immediate deployment of a centralized, digital  monitoring system explicitly tied to the 

138 
 
newly defined Key Performance Indicators (KPIs). The Committee is of the view that 
metrics evaluating resource efficiency, such as the downtime versus uptime of high-value 
life-saving assets like Linear Accelerator s and Cath Labs, must be strictly audited on a 
monthly basis. Furthermore, the Committee recommends that the Department enforce 
strict accountability regarding capacity management and service delivery targets. 
Indicators such as the Outpatient -to-Inpatient Conversion Rate, the 80 -90% Bed 
Occupancy Rate target, and the Trauma Survival Rate must be actively utilized to 
adjust administrative strategies dynamically, ensuring that the heavy investments in the 
Regional Cancer Centre and the new Advanced Trauma Ce ntre translate directly into a 
measurable reduction in patient waitlists and improved clinical outcomes.

training to complem ent preventive and palliative care approaches and improve 
affordability and accessibility of healthcare services. 
 
3.22.12 On being asked about the contribution of the Institute in alleviating the mental health

community engagement; and (f) Enhanced digital access and continuity of care.

3.22.19 The Committee takes into consideration the significant contribution of the 
NIMHANS, Bengaluru in strengthening the country‘s mental health ecosystem throu gh 
innovative digital platforms, decentralised service delivery, and large -scale capacity 
building initiatives. Programmes such as Tele -MANAS, the Digital Academy, and tele -
mentoring models for primary healthcare providers have demonstrated the potential o f 
technology-enabled systems to bridge the long -standing treatment gap, particularly in 
rural and underserved areas. However, considering the rising burden of mental health 
disorders and the limited availability of specialised professionals across the coun try, the 
Committee recommends that the Department further institutionalise and scale up such 
digital mental health platforms across all States and Union Territories. Strengthening 
Tele-MANAS with enhanced multilingual support, integration with district hos pitals 
and primary health centres, and linkage with the District Mental Health Programme 
(DMHP) would ensure timely crisis response, improved referral pathways, and 
continuity of care, thereby significantly expanding access to mental health services in 
remote and underserved regions. 
 
3.22.20 The Committee notes that community -based mental health models 
implemented by NIMHANS, including the Sakalawara Rural Psychiatry model, 
NAMAN programme, and tele -mentoring initiatives such as the ECHO model and 
Diploma in Primary Care Psychiatry (DPCP), have shown encouraging results in 
reducing treatment gaps, improving early detection, and empowering non -specialist 
healthcare providers. As such initiatives demonstrate that task -sharing approaches, 
combined with structu red training and community engagement, can effectively extend 
mental health services beyond tertiary care institutions. The Committee therefore 
recommends that the Department adopt these models more widely through integration 
with the National Health Missi on and the District Mental Health Programme, ensuring 
that trained primary care doctors, community health officers, ASHAs, and other 
frontline workers are equipped to identify and manage common mental health 

145 
 
conditions at the community level. Such decentra lised service delivery models would 
significantly reduce the burden on tertiary institutions while making mental healthcare 
more accessible and affordable for the population. 
 
3.22.21 The Committee further notes that several targeted interventions 
undertaken by NIMHANS, such as Yuva Spandana for youth mental health, SAMVAD 
for child protection and psychosocial care, USHAS –YASHAS for self -harm prevention, 
and specialised programmes in geriatric and perinatal mental health that have 
addressed critical and oft en under -recognised segments of the population. Given the 
growing prevalence of stress, anxiety, and self -harm among youth and vulnerable 
groups, the Committee recommends that the Department prioritise expansion of these 
life-cycle-based mental health prog rammes across the country through collaboration 
with educational institutions, community organisations, and state governments. 
Particular emphasis may be placed on strengthening school and college -based mental 
health support systems, expanding counselling services, and integrating psychosocial 
support within maternal and geriatric healthcare services.  
 
3.22.22 The Committee takes note of the policy announcements made in the Union 
Budget 2026 -27 regarding the establishment of a second national -level mental health 
institute in North India, the up -gradation of regional mental health institutes viz. 
Ranchi, Tezpur , other for decentralized specialist ca re, and the strengthening of 
emergency and trauma care centres with integrated psychiatric services. While thes e 
initiatives are expected to significantly enhance the country‘s mental healthcare 
infrastructure, the Committee emphasises the need for a coordinated implementation 
framework under the technical leadership of NIMHANS. The Committee recommends 
that the De partment ensure timely operationalisation of the proposed institute and 
regional upgrades while establishing strong academic, training, and digital linkages with 
NIMHANS to maintain uniform standards of care, research, and training across the 
network. In a ddition, NIMHANS may be entrusted with developing national protocols, 
quality benchmarks, and monitoring systems to guide the expansion of mental health 
services.  
 
3.22.23 The Committee recommends for integration of the Indian Knowledge 
System with modern medicine in a scientific and evidence -based manner to address the 
growing challenges of mental health in the country. Such integration, including the 
incorporation of traditional wellness practices, may complement existing treatment 
approaches, strengthen  preventive mental healthcare, and contribute to reducing the 
rising burden of mental health disorders.

CHAPTER IV 
 
NATIONAL HEALTH MISSION 
4.1 National Health Mission 
 
4.1.1   National Health Mission (NHM) aims for attainment of universal access to 
equitable, affordable and quality hea lth care services, accountable and responsive to people‘s 
needs, with effective inter -sectoral convergent action to address the wider social determinants of 
health. NHM enables the country to advance towards meeting Sustainable Development Goal 3, 
i.e. "Ensure healthy lives and promote well -being for all at all ages", including Universal Health 
Coverage. NHM consists of two Sub -Missions, the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) and 
the National Urban Health Mission (NUHM).  
 
4.1.2   The major objectives of NHM are as under:  
 
(i) Reduction in child and maternal mortality.  
(ii) Prevention and control of communicable and non -communicable diseases, 
including locally endemic diseases.  
(iii) Access to integrated comprehensive primary health care.  
(iv) Population stabilisation, gender equality and demographic balance.  
(v) Universal access to public services for food and nutrition, sanitation and hygiene 
and universal access to public health care services with emphasis on services 
addressing women‘s and children‘s health and universal immunisation.  
(vi) Promotion of healthy life styles.  
 
4.1.3   The main programmatic components include Health System Strengthening in 
rural and urban areas, Reproductive -Maternal- Neonatal-Child and Adolescent Health 
(RMNCH+A), an d Communicable and Non -Communicable Diseases. Under the NHM, 
technical and financial support is provided to State / UTs for strengthening of their healthcare 
systems based on the proposals submitted by them in their Programme Implementation Plans 
(PIPs). 
 
4.1.4 Under NHM, the performance of various health programmes including target sets

4.1.7 The Committee notes that the National Health Mission (NHM) has played a 
pivotal role in strengthening India‘s public health system and advancing progress 
towards the targets set under the National Health Policy, 2017 and Sustain able 
Development Goal -3. Significant improvements have been recorded in several health 
indicators, including an increase in life expectancy to 70.3 years, reduction in Infant 
Mortality Rate to 25 per thousand, Maternal Mortality Ratio to 88 per lakh live b irths, 
and high levels of immunisation coverage and antenatal care. The Committee 
appreciates the progress made in elimination of diseases such as Kala -Azar and 
sustained control of leprosy, along with improved TB treatment coverage. However, the 
Committee observes that certain targets, such as further reduction in under -five 
mortality, neonatal mortality, and improvement in family planning coverage, still 
require sustained attention. The Committee therefore recommends that the Department 
strengthen targeted interventions under NHM, particularly in States and districts that 
continue to lag behind national averages, through enhanced monitoring, data -driven 
planning, and focused support under Programme Implementation Plans (PIPs). Greater 
emphasis may also be placed on preventive healthcare, early detection of diseases, and 
behavioural change communication to consolidate the gains already achieved and 
accelerate progress towards remaining health targets. 
 
4.1.8 The Committee observe s the steady expansion of ser vices under the National 
Urban Health Mission (NUHM), with a significant increase in the number of Urban 
Primary Health Centres, polyclinics, Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, and healthcare 
personnel over the last three years, which has contributed to rising OPD a ttendance and 
improved service delivery in urban areas. While these developments indicate progress in 
strengthening urban health infrastructure, the Committee emphasises that rapid 
urbanisation, migration, and the growth of informal settlements continue to  place 
considerable pressure on urban public health systems. The Committee therefore 
recommends that the Department should strengthen the NUHM framework by ensuring 
adequate human resources, improving urban health infrastructure, and enhancing 
coordination with Urban Local Bodies to effectively address the healthcare needs of 

162 
 
vulnerable populations, including urban poor and migrant workers. The Committee also 
suggests expanding community participation through Mahila Arogya Samitis and 
ASHAs, and strengtheni ng initiatives such as free diagnostics, free drug services, and 
mobile medical units to ensure equitable and accessible healthcare services in urban 
areas.

4.1.15 The Committee notes tha t the expenditure under the National Health Mission 
(NHM) for FY 2024 –25 exceeded the Revised Estimates, indicating strong demand for 
financial resources and the critical role of the Mission in supporting public health 
systems across the country. However, the Committee also observes that in FY 2025 –26, 
the utilisation of funds up to 31.01.2026 stands at about 72.41 per cent of the Revised 
Estimates, which appears relatively low considering that only two months remain in the 
financial year. The Committee is of the view that such variations between allocation, 
utilisation, and actual expenditure point towards issues relating to financial planning, 
timely release of funds, and absorption capacity at the State/UT level. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Department must strengthen monitoring and 
coordination mechanisms with States/UTs to ensure timely submission of Programme 
Implementation Plans (PIPs), faster approval of Record of Proceedings (RoPs), and 
more efficient utilisation of allocated funds. The Committee also desires that the 
Department put in place a robust system for periodic review of expenditure trends so 
that mid -year corrections can be undertaken to avoid both underutilisation and 
overshooting of allocations. 
 
4.1.16 The Committee observes that a substantial portion of the allocation under NHM 
for FY 2026–27 is directed towards the Flexible Pool for Reproductive and Child Health 
(RCH), Health System Strengthening, National Health Programmes, and the National 
Urban Health Mission, which t ogether account for the major share of the total 
allocation. Given the expanding scope of services under the Ayushman Arogya Mandirs 
and the ongoing infrastructure development under the Pradhan Mantri Ayushman 
Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission, the Committee emphasises the need for sustained 
investments in strengthening primary healthcare infrastructure, human resources, and 
diagnostic capacities at the grassroots level. The Committee recommends that the 
Department prioritise effective implementation of these components by ensuring 
adequate staffing of health facilities, timely operationalisation of newly created 
infrastructure, and improved integration of digital health systems such as HMIS for 
real-time monitoring of service delivery. The Committee also  urges the Department to 
work closely with States/UTs to address regional disparities in health infrastructure and 
service delivery so that the benefits of NHM interventions reach vulnerable and 
underserved populations in both rural and urban areas.

the basis of provisional UCs of the previous financial year and the remaining 25% is subject

apprised of that no utilization certificate is pending under NHM.  On a query about the key

for public health facilities. These standards are linke d with well -defined assessment

tools and identified gaps are traversed through continual quality improvement methods

certification. The NQAS program aims to improve the credibility of public hospitals 
and recognize facilities that perform well.

an outlay of Rs. 64,180 Crores aims to support for infrastructure development for Sub-

surveillance and health research – spanning both the urban and rural areas. The

tertiary and on preparing health systems in responding effectively to the current and 
future pandemics/ disasters.

intake for undergraduates, enhancement of teacher -student ratio in PG etc which has 
resulted in substantial increase in number of undergraduate and post graduate seats.

4.1.20 Teleconsultation is expanding the reach to specialist care and enabling patients to 
connect with medical officers and specialists from remote locations. Teleconsultation 
platforms such as eSanjeevani and Tele MANAS facilitate real -time communication between 
patients and healthcare providers, allowing accurate and timely diagnosis, treatment planning, 
and follow -up care. This approach enhances the reach and quality of healthcare services, 
reduces Out-Of-Pocket Expenditure (OOPE) for patients with the need of long -distance travel 
in remote areas, and ensures timely consultations. Additionally, teleconsultation supports 
capacity building among primary care providers particularly the Community Health Officers 
(CHOs) and Auxiliary Nurse and Midwife (ANM) at the AAM-SHC by enabling them to seek 
guidance from specialists for handling the patients independently in future.  Ayushman Bharat 
Digital Mission (ABDM) launched in September 2021, aims to create the world‘s largest 
digital health ecosystem, supporting universal health cove rage and developing the backbone 
necessary to support the integrated digital health infrastructure of the country. ABDM 
envisages to create a secure online platform based on open, interoperable digital standards to 
bridge the existing gap amongst different stakeholders of healthcare ecosystem through digital 
pathways.

basis of provisional UCs and the remaining 25 per cent upon submission of audited UCs.

improvements in health infrastructure, quality of services and accessibility of healthcare 
facilities, particu larly in underserved regions. In this regard, the Committee 
recommends that the Department further strengthen its monitoring and evaluation 
mechanisms to ensure that the financial resources released under NHM translate into 
measurable improvements in servi ce delivery, especially through initiatives such as the 
National Quality Assurance Standards (NQAS), the Free Drugs and Free Diagnostics 
Service Initiatives, and teleconsultation platforms. The Committee also desires that the 
Department develop a comprehen sive outcome -based monitoring framework, linking 
financial releases with performance indicators such as quality certification of health 
facilities, availability of essential drugs and diagnostics, and reduction in Out -of-Pocket 
Expenditure (OOPE) for patients. 
 
4.1.22 The Committee further notes that despite the various initiatives undertaken by 
the Government under NHM, including incentives for medical professionals, multi -
skilling of doctors, expansion of medical education capacity and digital health init iatives 
such as teleconsultation and the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM), challenges 
related to shortage and uneven distribution of human resources, particularly in rural 
and remote areas, continue to persist. The Committee is of the considered view  that

recommends that the Department, in close coordination with States/UTs, intensify 
efforts to address the gaps in availability of doctors, specialists, nurses and paramedical

leverage digital health platforms, telemedicine services and the expanding network of

so that specialist consultations and referral services are seamlessly available at the 
primary healthcare level, thereby improving continuity of care and reducing the burden 
on secondary and tertiary healthcare facilities.

Development Goal target for Maternal Mortality Ratio, the Committee observes that 
disparities persist across regions and that high -burden districts continue to require 
focused attention. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department intensify 
targeted interventions in States and districts with relatively higher maternal and child 
mortality indicators by strengthening institutional delivery systems, improving referral 
transport and emergency obstetric care services, and enhancing community -based 
monitoring through frontline health workers. The Committee also urges the Department 
to leverage digital initiatives such as the proposed longitudinal health tracking system 
under Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram to ensure early identification of high -risk 
mothers and children, better follow -up care, and improved data -driven planning for 
maternal and child healthcare programmes across the country.

recommends that the Department pursue the immediate approval of the ₹496.16 crore

4.2.7 The Committee observes that while SSDRS 1.0 successfully expanded the

staggering 1,140 required stringent regulatory actions such as Stop Production Orders 
(SPOs) and licen se suspensions. The Committee believes that state -of-the-art testing

precondition for future fund disbursements. The Committee is of the view that the Risk -

nationwide to avoid pub lic health crisis occurred in Madhya Pradesh due to  
consumption of contaminated cough syrup. 
4.2.8 On being asked about the response of the Department to the proposal of centralized

activities of State Drug Control Organisations and provides expert advice through the Drugs 
Consultative Committee (DCC) meetings held with State Drugs Controllers for uniformity in 
administration of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act. This collaborative approach enables effective 
regulation and enforcement, leveraging both central and state expertise to ensure drug safety 
and quality in India.

4.2.13 On a specific query related to functioning of Central Drugs Standard Control 
Organisation (CDSCO), the Department stated that a s per information obtained from CDAC, 
during the last financial year, total number of manufacturing and import applications 
processed for Class C and Class D Medical Device are 2999 and out of these in approx. 62 
percent of applications queries were raised more than twice. Further, out of 1677 import 
applications, 1060 applications belong to Class -C and Class D Medical Devices having 
USFDA/CE certificate. In this, 253 such applications are under process for more than 90 
days. Most of these applications are pending at the applicants end for submission of r equisite 
documents as per MDR-2017.  
 
4.2.14 The Committee notes with concern the significant administrative bottlenecks 
hindering the swift clearance of medical devices, particularly the Class C and Class D 
categories regulated by the Central Drugs Standa rd Control Organisation (CDSCO). 
The Committee observes that out of 2,999 manufacturing and import applications 
processed, approximately 62% were subjected to queries more than twice, and 253 
import applications, even those possessing USFDA/CE certificatio ns, have been pending 
for over 90 days. The Committee believes that such repetitive query cycles indicate a 
systemic lack of clarity in the initial submission guidelines and point toward an 
inefficient, iterative assessment process. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
Department immediately overhaul the 'MD Online' portal to include a mandatory, AI -
assisted pre-submission validation checklist to ensure applications are complete before 
formal submission. The Committee is of the view that CDSCO must  adopt a "single 
comprehensive query" policy, wherein all deficiencies in an application are identified 
and communicated to the applicant in a single instance, rather than in piece -meal 
fashion. The Committee, furthermore, recommends the establishment of a  dedicated 

174 
 
facilitation cell within CDSCO to assist domestic manufacturers in navigating the 
Medical Device Rules (MDR) 2017, thereby reducing the delays currently attributed to 
pending applicant responses. 
 
4.2.15 The Committee acknowledges the constituti onally mandated decentralized 
framework where State Authorities regulate drugs and Class A/B devices, while the 
Centre oversees imports and Class C/D devices. The Committee recommends for a 
decentralized framework for imports and Class  C/D devices . The Com mittee strongly 
recommends that CDSCO approval for imports be completely decentralized to the State 
Authorities. Centralization with the DGCI  at the Central level has created major 
bottlenecks and is the biggest hurdle in India being at the forefront of Me dical devices 
manufacturing. The Committee recommends for decentralization of approval for all 
Medical Devices with the State Drug Authorities to reduce pendency. In this current 
phase when we are competing with China, Vietnam, Malaysia giving CDSCO approv als 
for even already approved devices/ technologies beyond a period of 45 days in resulting 
in India losing its competitive edge.  
 
4.2.16 The Committee further observes that CDSCO has generated substantial revenue 
from medical device licensing, collecting  between ₹87.18 crore and ₹118.69 crore 
annually over the last three financial years. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the revenue earned should be used for self -financing of the Institution. A designated 
percentage of the revenue collected by CDS CO be ring -fenced and directly reinvested 
into upgrading the digital and technical infrastructure of both the Central and State 
regulatory bodies. The Committee is of the view that the Department must utilize these 
funds to develop a unified, real -time Nat ional Regulatory Dashboard that seamlessly 
integrates CDSCO‘s 'MD Online' portal with State -level licensing databases. This will 
ensure that intelligence regarding non -compliant manufacturers, suspended licenses, 
and spurious drug trails is instantly share d across jurisdictions, leveraging both central 
and state expertise to guarantee uniform enforcement of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 
nationwide.

have been approved but out of that 137 Medical College s are functional, with expansion 
of MBBS seats in existing institutions, and the creatio n of postgraduate medical seats 
across the country. While appreciating the initiatives, the Committee is of the view that 
timely completion and operationalisation of approved institutions are essential for 
translating financial allocations into tangible im provements in healthcare manpower. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department strengthen monitoring and 
coordination with States/UTs to ensure timely submission of DPRs, completion of 
infrastructure projects, recruitment of faculty and adhere nce to funding conditions 
under the SNA -SPARSH framework so that the approved medical colleges and 
expanded seats become fully functional within the stipulated timelines.  There is need to

comprehensive approach towards s trengthening the entire healthcare workforce by 
simultaneously expanding medical, nursing and allied health education capacities,

MISSION (PM-ABHIM) 
4.5.1 The PM-Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission (PM -ABHIM) was launched 
on 25th October, 2021 with an outlay of Rs.64,180 Cr to be implemented over five years from 
2021-22 to 2025-26, with the aim to strengthen the public health infrastructure to fill critical 
gaps in health infrastructure, surveillance and health research - spanning both the urban and  
rural areas. The objectives of the scheme are as follows: 
i. To develop capacities of health systems and institutions across the continuum of 
care at all levels viz. primary, secondary and tertiary. 
ii. To strengthen grass root public health institutions to deli ver universal 
comprehensive primary health care and governance capacities for comprehensive 
diagnostic and treatment including for critical care services.  

186 
 
iii. To expand and build an IT enabled disease surveillance system by developing a 
network of surveillanc e laboratories for effectively detecting, investigating, 
preventing and combating Public Health Emergencies and Disease Outbreaks. 
 
4.5.2 PM-ABHIM is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme with Central Sector Components. The 
envisaged targets under the CSS component s (including XV -FC share) of the scheme 
includes: 
i. Infrastructure Support for 17,788 Rural building -less Sub Health Centers -Health 
and Wellness Centers, now renamed as Ayushman Arogya Mandir (AAM). 
ii. Establishment of 11,024 Urban Health and Wellness Centers ( Ayushman Arogya 
Mandir) in all the States with a focus on slum and slum like areas. 
iii. Establishment of 3382 Block Public Health Units at block levels. 
iv. Setting up of 730 Integrated Public Health Labs in all districts across the Country. 
v. Establishment of 602 Critical Care Blocks in all the districts with population more 
than 5 lakhs and referral linkages in other districts.  
 
4.5.3 The Committee notes that the Pradhan Mantri Ayushman Bharat Health 
Infrastructure Mission (PM-ABHIM) was launched with a substantia l outlay of ₹64,180 
crore for the period 2021 –22 to 2025 –26 with the objective of strengthening public 
health infrastructure across primary, secondary and tertiary levels of care. The Mission 
envisages a wide range of infrastructure interventions including  construction of 
building-less Sub -Health Centres as Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, establishment of 
Urban Health and Wellness Centres, Block Public Health Units, Integrated Public 
Health Laboratories and Critical Care Hospital Blocks across districts. While 
appreciating the comprehensive design of the Mission aimed at strengthening health 
systems, surveillance networks and emergency preparedness, the Committee is of the 
view that the success of such a large -scale initiative depends on timely completion of 
infrastructure, operationalisation of facilities and adequate human resources and 
equipment support. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department 
strengthen coordination and monitoring mechanisms with States/UTs to ensure timely 
completion of sanctio ned infrastructure, adherence to project timelines and optimal 
utilisation of funds so that the envisaged public health facilities become fully functional 
at the earliest to facilitate healthcare of the global standard.

a) PM-ABHIM is a capital -intensive infrastructure scheme involving construction, 
renovation, procurement of equipment, and establishment of facilities across

always align evenly with annual budget estimates.

utilization of funds under the PM -ABHIM scheme, evidenced by the severe reduction of 
the 2025–26 Budget Estimate from ₹4,200.00 crore to a Revised Estimate of ₹2,442.50 
crore, of which only 59% had been utilized by January 2026. The Co mmittee believes 
that while the onboarding of all 31 States and UTs onto the SNA -SPARSH platform is a 
necessary financial reform for transparency, but such transition should not become a 
perennial bottleneck that stalls the rollout of critical health infra structure. The 
Committee, therefore, desires that the Department should immediately deploy dedicated 
Task Forces. These task forces must move beyond basic capacity building and actively 
assist state treasuries in mapping implementing agencies, reconciling unspent balances, 
and expediting the fulfillment of conditions required for subsequent lump -sum releases. 
The Committee is of the view that until the SNA -SPARSH system is fully stabilized, the 
Department should conditionally ease procedural rigidities to e nsure that fund flows for 
life-saving infrastructure are not artificially constricted. 
4.5.8 The Committee observes that the fundamental delays in executing PM -ABHIM 
are consistently attributed to the gestation periods inherent in capital -intensive projects, 
including the preparation of Detailed Project Reports (DPRs), land acquisition, and 
state-specific tendering processes across various components like Integrated Public 
Health Laboratories (IPHLs) and Critical Care Hospital Blocks (CCHBs). The 
Committee believes that leaving States entirely to their own administrative capacities to 
navigate these complex pre -construction phases inevitably leads to the highly uneven 
physical and financial progress currently observed. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends th at the Department establish a centralized 'Infrastructure Project 
Management Unit' (IPMU) strictly dedicated to PM -ABHIM. This unit should provide 
States with pre -approved, standardized DPR templates, centralized architectural 
blueprints, and model tenderi ng documents to bypass local bureaucratic inertia. 
Furthermore, the Committee is of the view that future fund releases must be linked to 
centrally monitored timelines for land allotment and human resource recruitment, 
ensuring that once physical infrastruc ture is erected, it does not lie dormant due to a 
lack of specialized medical personnel. 
4.5.9 On a query regarding the allocation of ₹4,200 crore at the BE stage for 2026 –27 under 
the scheme, despite the PM -ABHIM being originally envisaged for implementation over a 
five-year period from 2021–22 to 2025–26, the Department stated that: 
a) PM-ABHIM is  a capital -intensive infrastructure initiative aimed at strengthening 
public health facilities up to the block level. Given the nature of construction, 
procurement, and upgradation activities, the scheme entails inherent gestation periods, 
which resulted i n relatively lower expenditure during the initial years of 
implementation. As the scheme has now reached at an advanced stage, with a 
substantial number of projects under execution and nearing completion, expenditure is 
expected to accelerate in line with implementation progress.  
b) The allocation of Rs. 4,200 crore in BE 2026 -27 has been made keeping in view the 
scheme‘s committed liabilities, and the anticipated scale -up and completion of 

190 
 
ongoing projects, rather than past expenditure trends alone. The prov ision is intended 
to ensure continuity of works already approved and to meet financial requirements 
arising from physical progress on the ground. Further, EFC document for extension of 
the scheme has been circulated & proposal is under consideration. 
c) The Ministry continuously reviews State/UT-wise physical and financial progress, the 
pipeline of approved projects, utilization patterns, and implementation readiness 
through regular review meetings and Common Review Missions. Budgetary 
projections are aligned with realistic absorptive capacity and the requirement to 
complete approved deliverables within the approved framework of the scheme.

4.6 AYUSHMAN BHARAT -PRADHAN MANTRI JAN AROGYA YOJANA (AB -

4.6.1 Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri – Jan Arogya Yojana (AB PM -JAY) is the world‘s 
largest health assurance scheme that intends to reduce the out -of-pocket expenditure arising 
due to catastrophic expenditure on healthcare. AB PM-JAY was launched on 23rd September, 
2018 as recommended by the National Health Policy 2017, to achieve the SDGs vision of 
Universal Health Coverage (UHC), subsuming the erstwhile Ras htriya Swasthya Bima 
Yojana (RSBY). The scheme provides health cover of ₹ 5 lakhs per family per year for 
secondary and tertiary care hospitalization to bottom 40% of the India‘s poor and vulnerable 
population.

4.6.6 The Committee observes that as of January 2026, 33,271 hospitals have been 
empanelled, with a split between public (17,508) and private (15,763) institutions. While 
the creation of 43.17 crore Ayushman Cards is commendable, the Co mmittee believes 
that the true efficacy of the scheme lies in the "portability" and "cashless" nature of the 
services delivered. The Committee is concerned that with 11.46 crore authorized 
hospital admissions, the pressure on the existing network of 33,271  hospitals will 
intensify considering the inclusion of senior citizens. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Department launch a targeted drive to empanel more private 
tertiary care specialty hospitals, particularly in underserved and remote areas, to reduce 
the travel burden for vulnerable populations. Furthermore, the Committee is of the view 
that the Department must institutionalize a robust, real -time "Patient Satisfaction and 
Outcome Audit" to ensure that the "completely paperless and cashless " promise is 
strictly adhered to on the ground, preventing any instances of unauthorized out -of-
pocket charges at the point of care. 
4.6.7 On being asked for the reasons of increasing allocation ₹ 9,500 crore in BE 2026 -27, 
the Department stated that u nder AB PMJA Y, the budget requirement is estimated based on 
the number of eligible beneficiary families and fixed annual premium of ₹1,052 per family 
per year. As the AB PMJAY is a Centrally Sponsore d Scheme, the cost is shared between the 
Centre and the States. Accordingly, the budget for the core AB PMJAY beneficiary family 
base for 12 crore families remains a committed and largely fixed liability. Further, in FY 
2024-25, coverage under AB PM -JAY wa s expanded to include approximately 37 lakh 
families of ASHA, AWW and AWH workers, as well as about 4.5 crore senior citizen 
families aged 70 years and above.  
4.6.8 During FY 2025–26, a total central share of ₹ 7,093.51 crore has been released so far 
to t he States/UTs based on demands raised. Of this, ₹ 307.87 crore has been released for 
Ayushman Vay Vandana category, and ₹ 47.89 crore under the ASHA/AWW/AWH category 
during FY 2025-26. However, several States/UTs have not yet raised demands for the central  
share under Ayushman Vay Vandana and ASHA/AWW/AWH category due to various 
implementation related challenges.  It is expected that the pending demands for FY 2025 –26, 
along with the regular demands for FY 2026 –27, will be raised in the subsequent financial 
year. Further, the expansion of beneficiary groups under Ayushman Vay Vandana and 
ASHA/AWW/AWH has led to an increase in Ayushman Card creation, hospital admissions, 
and claims submission. In view of this rising utilisation and expanded beneficiary base, 
demands from States/UTs are expected to increase in FY 2026 –27, and th erefore the 
enhanced Budget Estimate of ₹ 9,500 crore is expected to be fully utilised.  
4.6.9 On being asked the percentage of funds have been utilised for rural and tribal areas, it 
is submitted that an amount of Rs. 320.00 crore has been surrendered und er the North Eastern

a) To address these challenges and strengthen outreach, NHA is undertaking extensive

to States for corrective action.

4.6.16 On a specific query related to fraud cases and irregularities under the scheme, it is 
submitted that NHA follows a zero -tolerance approach towards fraud under AB PM -JAY. 
The National Anti-Fraud Unit (NAFU), uses AI/ML -based automated triggers to flag unusual 
claim patterns such as duplicate entries, inflated procedures, or misuse of  patient identity, etc. 
All submitted claims are subjected to fraud and abuse analytics within 24 hours of c laim 
submission by hospitals. Claims that are identified suspicious through system -based analytics 
and triggers are flagged and forwarded to the respective State Anti -Fraud Units (SAFUs) for 
further verification and detailed investigation. 
4.6.17 Some of t he major categories of abuse/fraud identified through these system -based 
checks include Medical Identity Theft (such as use of duplicate or forged patient images), 
billing for services not rendered (e.g. Duplicate claim raised for a patient on same day), 
upcoding or unbundling of services (where higher -value packages are claimed or bundled 
services are split to seek excess reimbursement), deviation from Standard Treatment 
Guidelines (STGs), etc. As on 21 January 2026, cases involving fraud and abuse amounting to 
₹644.04 crore have been prevented through rejection of the associated claims prior to 
payment, thereby safeguarding public funds. Further, a near real -time dedicated anti -fraud 
dashboard has been developed to enhance monitoring and oversight at the S tate/UT level. In 
addition, regular capacity -building workshops and field -level training programmes are 
conducted for States/UTs to strengthen the anti -fraud framework and reinforce compliance 
among all stakeholders. The year -wise status of total claims su bmitted and claims identified

4.6.19 On being asked about the data that supports maintaining the current ₹5 lakh cap for

that the existing ₹ 5 lakh limit is adequate to meet the hospitalisation needs of the vast

4.6.20 It is further submitted that the senior citizen category under AB PM -JAY was

NHA, for senior citizen benefici ary families, for the FY 2025 -26, more than 91% of families 
have utilized less than ₹1 lakh of wallet. In view of this, it appears that  existing ₹ 5 lakh per

including those with comorbidities. Further, the scheme design allows beneficiaries with 
comorbid conditions to avail multiple procedures within a single pre -authorisation. In view of 
the above, no separate estimation of additional budgetary requirement for intro duction of a

4.6.21 The Committee notes the enhanced allocation of ₹9,500 crore for FY 2026 –27 under 
Ayushman Bharat –Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB PM -JAY) in view of the 
expansion of beneficiary categories, including senior citizens aged 70 years and above and 
frontline workers such as ASHA, AWW and AWH. The Committee is of the view that while 

199 
 
the scheme has contributed to reducing out -of-pocket expenditure and has enabled a large 
number of cashless hospitalisations across the country, the Committee observes that 
challenges remain in terms of outreach, timely claim settlement, and adequacy of coverage 
for critical and high-cost treatments.  
 
4.6.22 The Committee reiterates its recommend ation that the Department undertake a 
comprehensive review of the scheme with a view t o further widening coverage, including 
rationalisation of the eligibility criteria for senior citizens by considering lowering the age 
threshold from 70 years to 60 years irrespective of socio -economic status. The Committee 
also recommends that the Departm ent evaluate the feasibility of enhancing the existing 
insurance cover from ₹5 lakh to ₹10 lakh limit in view of rising medical costs and expensive 
tertiary care interventions. Further, the Department may review and expand the list of 
procedures and diagno stics covered under the scheme, particularly high -end investigations 
such as CT scans, MRI and nuclear imaging, as well as advanced treatments for critical 
illnesses, so as to ensure that beneficiaries receive comprehensive and financially protected 
healthcare services without being compelled to incur additional out-of-pocket expenditure. 
 
4.6.23 The Committee notes that the Government had announced the inclusion of gig and 
platform workers under the scheme with the objective of extending health protection to this 
emerging segment of the workforce,  however, the Committee is constrained to observe that 
the proposal has not yet been operationalised as the matter is stated to be under 
consideration with the Ministry of Labour and Employment. The Committee empha sises 
that gig and platform workers constitute a rapidly growing section of the labour force that 
often lack access to formal social security and health coverage. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Department take up the matter with the Ministry  of Labour and 
Employment on priority so that the modalities for identification, enrolment and coverage of 
gig and platform workers are finalised expeditiously and the scheme is implemented without 
further delay. Early operationalisation of this initiative  would help extend the benefits of 
financial protection in healthcare to a vulnerable and expanding workforce segment and 
strengthen the overall objective of inclusive health coverage. 
 
4.6.24 The Committee further notes that despite the growing utilisatio n of the scheme, 
several implementation -related challenges persist, including delays in raising demand by 
some States/UTs, limited awareness among eligible beneficiaries, and occasional delays in 
settlement of claims of empanelled hospitals. The Committee , therefore, recommends the 
Department to intensify awareness and outreach campaigns across rural, tribal and remote 
areas so that eligible families are fully informed about the benefits of the scheme and are not 
left out from enrolment.  
 
4.6.25 The Commit tee further recommends that the Department should strengthen 
coordination with States/UTs to ensure timely raising of claims and efficient utilisation of 
allocated funds, particularly in regions where utilisation remains low. The Committee 
further recommen ds that the Department to streamline and strictly monitor the claim 
settlement mechanism to ensure that payments to empanelled hospitals are processed within 
the stipulated timelines. In addition, the package rates under the scheme may be periodically 

200 
 
reviewed in consultation with States/UTs and healthcare providers so as to maintain 
financial viability for hospitals and prevent denial of treatment to beneficiaries. Such 
measures would enhance the effectiveness, transparency and sustainability of the scheme  
while ensuring equitable access to quality healthcare for all eligible citizens. 
 
4.6.26 The Committee observes that the effectiveness of the scheme is closely linked to the 
availability and equitable distribution of empanelled hospitals and quality healt hcare 
infrastructure across States/UTs. The Committee wish es to highlight that although a large 
number of hospitals have been empanelled under the scheme, but there continue to be 
regional disparities, particularly in rural, aspirational and remote areas w here access to 
empanelled facilities remains limited. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
Department, in coordination with States/UTs, take proactive measures to expand the 
network of empanelled public and private hospitals in underserved regions  so that 
beneficiaries do not have to travel long distances to avail treatment. The Committee also 
emphasises the need to strengthen public health institutions and encourage their greater 
participation under the scheme, along with periodic quality audits o f empanelled facilities to 
ensure adherence to prescribed standards of care. Such steps would enhance accessibility, 
improve service delivery and ensure that the benefits of the scheme reach beneficiaries 
across all regions in an equitable manner. 
 
4.6.27 The Committee notes that the success of the scheme also depends on robust 
monitoring, transparency and effective use of digital platforms for beneficiary identification, 
hospital empanelment and claim processing. While the Department has developed IT -based 
systems for implementation and monitoring, the Committee is of the view that there is scope 
for further strengthening data analytics and real -time monitoring mechanisms to detect 
irregularities, prevent fraudulent claims and improve overall efficiency of the scheme. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department to  strengthen the digital ecosystem 
of the scheme by integrating advanced analytics, periodic audits and grievance redressal 
mechanisms so as to ensure transparency and accountability in  its implementation. The 
Committee desires that feedback received from beneficiaries and empanelled hospitals be 
systematically collected and analysed to identify operational issues and improve service 
delivery under the scheme. Such measures would help in  ensuring that the scheme functions 
in a transparent, efficient and beneficiary -centric manner while safeguarding public 
resources.

5.1 PROMOTION OF INDIGENOUS MEDICAL TECHNOLOGY AND EASING 
REGULATIONS 
 
5.1.1 On being asked what measures are proposed in 2026 –27 for promoting indigenous 
medical technology, rationalising duties/taxes, easing regulations, and improving affordability 
and accessibility of healthcare, the Department submitted that the Government  is making 
efforts to reduce the OOPE as a percentage of Total Health Expenditure (THE). There has 
been a significant increase in Government Health Expenditure (GHE) as percentage of THE, 
which has increased from 29.0% in 2014-15 to 48.0% in 2021-22.  
5.1.2 Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has rolled out and implemented various 
schemes and programs to provide accessible, affordable and quality healthcare services to all, 
including those in rural areas. These key schemes/programs have contributed in red ucing out-
of-pocket expenditures in availing health services, some of these initiatives are National 
Health Mission (NHM): Ayushman Arogya Mandir (AAM) : Pradhan Mantri Ayushman 
Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission ( PM-ABHIM) Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri  Jan 
Arogya Yojana (AB-PMJAY).  
5.1.3 Besides, quality generic medicines are made available at affordable prices to all under 
Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana (PMBJP) in collaboration with the State 
Governments. Affordable Medicines and Relia ble Implants for Treatment (AMRIT) 
Pharmacy stores have been set up in some hospitals/Institutions.―Make in India‖ guidelines 
are followed for procurement and indigenous technologies are introduced in public health 
system from time to time depending on req uirement, regulatory approval, recommendation of 
Health Technology Assessment Board under DHR and feasibility of implementation.  
5.1.4 The Committee consider s that the Department should adopt a coordinated 
strategy in 2026 –27 to promote indigenous medical  technology while simultaneously 
improving affordability and accessibility of healthcare. This should include prioritising 
procurement under ―Make in India‖ guidelines, rationalising duties and taxes on 
essential medical devices and drugs, and streamlining  regulatory approvals through a 
single-window mechanism to encourage innovation and faster adoption.
